title: Belowground Productivity in Grasslands and Savannas Depends on Shifting Fire and Herbivory Regimes
content:
Long-term experiments across a climate gradient show belowground net primary productivity (BNPP) in grasslands and savannas depends on fire and herbivory. Disturbance stimulated BNPP in wet savannas by limiting woody thickening and promoting herbaceous growth while drier sites remained resilient, revealing climate-disturbance effects belowground have major implications for carbon storage.


ABSTRACT

In grasslands and savannas, most plant biomass and net primary productivity is belowground. How shifts in disturbance regimes, such as fire or large herbivore activity, impact belowground net primary productivity (BNPP) is unclear across climate-driven productivity gradients. We tested the hypothesis that altered fire and herbivory regimes impact BNPP by changing the relative biomass of herbaceous and woody plants, which differ in their relative allocation to BNPP, and that climate constrains how much disturbance shifts this herbaceous–woody balance. We measured BNPP and aboveground vegetation across seven African and North American grasslands and savannas, with three long-term fire manipulation levels (high frequency, intermediate frequency, and suppressed) and, at six sites, two long-term herbivory levels (large herbivores excluded or open to large herbivores). Sites spanned an aridity index (mean annual precipitation [mm]/potential evapotranspiration [mm]) gradient—and associated woody thickening potential—from 0.21 to 0.71. BNPP increased with water availability. Fire and herbivory increased BNPP, with greater effects in wetter sites. In the wettest sites, BNPP gains under disturbance correlated with herbaceous biomass gains, as herbivory and frequent fire reduced woody plant cover relative to disturbance exclusion plots. BNPP responses were also predicted by root biomass, explaining why wetter sites and frequently disturbed plots within sites had higher BNPP. Climate determined how much the positive response of root biomass offset fire and grazing reductions in aboveground plant stocks, largely because water availability constrained the total aboveground plant biomass achieved without disturbance. Therefore, disturbances stimulated BNPP in wet savannas, largely by limiting woody thickening and promoting herbaceous growth with higher BNPP rates, whereas BNPP in drier and mesic sites tended to be resilient. Our findings show that belowground processes in grasslands and savannas fundamentally depend on disturbance regimes, climate-driven productivity gradients, and their interactions, with important implications for understanding global carbon storage.
